[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p177/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · حمزة والكسائي وابن عامر | reports | Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Ibn ʿĀmir follow the light-vowel rule for the pronoun hā; only Ḥafṣ's transmissions from ʿĀṣim are said to lengthen the kasra in the listed exceptions. | mentions 18:63, 48:10, 25:69
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p177/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathīr connects hā with yā after yā, wāw, alif, or any still or moving letter, and with waw after the corresponding vowel contexts. | mentions 22:4, 18:63, 52:28, 16:121
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p177/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو بكر محمد بن السري | prefers | Abū Bakr ibn al-Sarrī prefers kasra without yā or assimilation in فيه; Abū Ḥātim calls this the common reading, and the consonant skeleton also lacks yā.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p177/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو بكر محمد بن السري | rejects | He rejects assimilation after kasra: the kasra implies an intended yā, while an actual yā separates the two hāʾs; their assimilation is also heavy.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p177/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو حاتم | reports | Abū Ḥātim reports that Nāfiʿ assimilated the two hāʾs with a trace of ḍamma, and argues that Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr only lightly colored the hā rather than adding a glide.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p177/r8] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو حاتم | holds | Abū Ḥātim says ḍamma is a recognized dialect without a spoken waw; adding waw or yā would separate the hāʾs and prevent assimilation.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p177/r9] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · بعض أصحابنا | reports | Some colleagues judge assimilation heavy in pronunciation but valid by analogy because the hāʾs share an articulation point; throat letters and a word boundary make it awkward.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p179/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash reports assimilation of the two hāʾs in فيه هدى as a reading.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p179/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو بكر | rejects | Abū Bakr says true assimilation cannot coexist with a vowel or separation; Abū ʿAmr instead made a quick, concealed vowel that listeners mistook for assimilation.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p179/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو حاتم | holds | Abū Ḥātim says Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr intended concealment, not full assimilation, since genuine assimilation would silence the first hā; Abū ʿAmr avoided excessive movement and full vowels.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p179/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh distinguishes أراب, to become a possessor of doubt, from رابني, to put me into doubt, comparing the first pattern to becoming deserving of blame.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p179/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو زيد | reports | Abū Zayd says رابني describes a witnessed matter that makes doubt certain, whereas أرابني describes suspicion without certainty; a poem illustrates the latter.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p179/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda glosses لا ريب as no doubt.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p179/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh notes that a shortened verbal noun of this pattern is rare except with weak roots, and explains هدى as an exceptional source form of هديته.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p181/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Al-Fārisī allows هدى to be a source form confined to weak roots, like كينونة, though the corresponding source pattern is absent from sound roots.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p181/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | He notes that words not normally classified as verbal nouns can function like sources, citing Labīd's construction as an object governed like a source.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p181/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | On this usage, هدى, سرى, and تقى can stand in for a source, as تقاة does in 3:28; the cited poetic usage likewise treats a noun as a source. | mentions 3:28
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p181/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda explains هدى للمتقين as clarification for the God-fearing.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p181/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو الحسن | reports | Abū al-Ḥasan reports that some Arabs treat هدى as feminine.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p181/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The verb هدى takes two objects; its second object may be introduced by إلى or لام, as the cited Qurʾanic examples show. | mentions 37:23, 38:22, 43:43, 10:35, 16:68, 99:5
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p181/r8] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | When the preposition is omitted, اهدنا الصراط means show us the path and lead us on it; the request seeks the guidance promised to followers of God's good pleasure. | mentions 1:6, 5:16, 6:127
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p184/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | دار السلام may be an honorific genitive referring to God's name al-Salām, like بيت الله or عبد الله.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p184/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Alternatively, دار السلام means the abode of safety, where residents suffer neither hardship nor punishment, as 35:35 describes. | mentions 35:35, 37:23, 57:13
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p184/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Asking for the straight path can mean asking for firmness in faith and the ways of religion, avoiding those who have strayed; 6:153 and 37:117–118 reinforce this reading. | mentions 5:77, 60:1, 6:153, 37:117, 37:118
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p184/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The other interpretation asks for direction to Paradise and reward, supported by the promise to guide those slain in God's path and set their affairs right. | mentions 47:4, 47:5
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p186/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو الحسن | reports | Abū al-Ḥasan distinguishes guiding a bride to her husband from presenting her as a gift; Tamīm uses the former form while Qays uses the latter.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p186/r10] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أحمد | reports | Aḥmad treats هدى and أهدى as equivalent, citing a poem in which a speaker tells a woman to give him meat.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p186/r11] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Abū ʿAlī says the singular of الهدي is هدية, by analogy with مطي and مطية, and cites a poem about garlanded offerings.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p186/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو الحسن | reports | The opposition of guidance and misguidance supports glossing الهدى as direction or guidance. | mentions 2:198
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p186/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن مقبل | reports | Ibn Muqbil's poem uses أهدي for guiding others, contrasting it with not being guided himself.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p186/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | reports | In the cited desert poem, استبنت الهدى means daylight became clear; the mirage makes the distant desert and camels appear to rise and sink.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p186/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abū ʿAmr glosses غلفا as having nothing that covers the camels and explains يصلينا as their seeming to burn while the mirage lifts and lowers them.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p186/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أحمد بن يحيى | reports | Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā reports Baghdad usage of هدي بيت الله; Hijaz speakers lighten الهدي while Tamīm gives it a heavier pronunciation, and its singular is هدية. | mentions 2:196
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p186/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | reports | Both vocalic forms are read in the phrase about the sacrificial offering reaching its place in 2:196. | mentions 2:196
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p186/r8] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Calling someone the هدي of a tribe means its protected neighbor, whose harm is forbidden like that of a sacrificial offering.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p186/r9] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The derivatives cover offering a sacrifice or a gift, escorting a bride, the direction of a matter, demeanor, guiding a lost animal or a person to religion, a generous giver, and a gift tray.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p188/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | فيه may be the predicate of لا ريب, raised as the predicate of the subject under Sībawayh's analysis or as the predicate of إن under Abū al-Ḥasan's.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p188/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Alternatively, فيه is an adjective with an omitted predicate; it is accusative if the adjective follows the surface form, but raised if it follows the syntactic position. | mentions 12:92
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p188/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The case belongs to the adverbial phrase itself, not the omitted word it modifies, because the pronoun is contained in the adverb.
[BAQILLANI:v1p22/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | If the opponents could match the Qur’an, rational custom makes their abandoning an easy decisive reply for harder hostility implausible.

 | Their eloquence and expertise, together with repeated public taunts about their incapacity, should have driven them to answer if able.

[BAQILLANI:v1p22/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | He includes the Qur’an’s description as guidance for the God-fearing among its declarations magnifying its status.

[SULAMI:v1p47#2/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · قيل | reports | One reading makes the Book the decree written for creation concerning felicity, wretchedness, lifespan, and provision; no one can alter it.
[SULAMI:v1p47#2/r10] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو يزيد | reports | Abu Yazid defines the God-fearing person as one who speaks and acts for God.
[SULAMI:v1p47#2/r11] SULAMI, d. 412 · الداراني | reports | Al-Darani defines the God-fearing as those whose hearts have been stripped of love for desires.
[SULAMI:v1p47#2/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · قيل | reports | Another reading makes the Book God's love and knowledge inscribed in the hearts of His friends, with contentment toward the events of His decree.
[SULAMI:v1p47#2/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · قيل | reports | The Book is the covenant to the Beloved and place of the secret; the Prophet knows revelation's mysteries, and saints and truthful ones after him love its subtleties.
[SULAMI:v1p47#2/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · قيل | reports | A further reading is the pre-eternal divine pledge that God's mercy preceded His wrath.
[SULAMI:v1p47#2/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · قيل | reports | There is no doubt for the person whose secret God opens and whose heart He adorns with understanding from Him.
[SULAMI:v1p47#2/r6] SULAMI, d. 412 · قيل | reports | There is no doubt for the person whose secret is purified by the light of insight into the text's subtle meanings.
[SULAMI:v1p47#2/r7] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | For the people of gnosis, the Book is true guidance and an added clarification.
[SULAMI:v1p47#2/r8] SULAMI, d. 412 · سهل | reports | Sahl calls it clarification for someone who magnifies his own affairs, power, and strength.
[SULAMI:v1p47#2/r9] SULAMI, d. 412 · الجنيد | reports | Junayd reads the guidance as connection for those cut off from created entities.
[THALABI:v1p139/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو عمرو | reports | The general readers pronounce Dhalika with an open dhal; Abu Amr also permits imala in the dhal of hadhihi.
[THALABI:v1p139/r13] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | In Dhalika, dhal is the noun, lam is a support element, and kaf marks address; the demonstrative points to something absent.
[THALABI:v1p140/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Al-kitab means the written object, as in the words hisab and imad; the poet's reference to a page that has come to the addressee with its writing illustrates this usage.
[THALABI:v1p140/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · يمان بن رئاب | reports | Yaman ibn Ri'ab says it is the book mentioned in the Torah and Gospel.
[THALABI:v1p140/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Sa'id ibn Jubayr identifies the book as the Preserved Tablet.
[THALABI:v1p140/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · عكرمة | reports | Ikrima says the book means the Torah, Gospel, and earlier scriptures.
[THALABI:v1p140/r13] THALABI, d. 427 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra says God had promised the Prophet a book that water would not erase and repeated recitation would not wear out; when the Quran came, God identified it as the promised book.
[THALABI:v1p140/r14] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن كيسان | reports | Ibn Kaysan takes the book to mean the Quranic material before al-Baqara, since the disbelievers had rejected the dozen or so suras revealed before it.
[THALABI:v1p140/r15] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Another reported view identifies the book as the one denied by the Jewish figure Malik ibn al-Sayf.
[THALABI:v1p140/r16] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | La rayba fihi means there is no doubt that the Quran comes from God.
[THALABI:v1p140/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The noun kitab derives from joining letters together; the root also describes sewing beads into two parts, and the cited verse uses al-katb for the stitching.
[THALABI:v1p140/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · ذو المرجة | reports | Dhu al-Marja's line uses al-katb to mean the joining or stitching between parts of a garment.
[THALABI:v1p140/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The author also notes that kataba can mean marking or branding a mule, and that a troop is called a katiba, plural kataib.
[THALABI:v1p140/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | A poet's line about a katiba provides usage evidence for the word meaning troop.
[THALABI:v1p140/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس والحسن وقتادة ومجاهد والضحاك ومقاتل | reports | Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil say the book is the Quran; on this view Dhalika means this, as in the cited demonstrative about Abraham's proof. | mentions 6:83
[THALABI:v1p140/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Khaffaf ibn Nudba's line uses dhalika in the sense of hadha, this.
[THALABI:v1p140/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Abu al-Duha transmits Ibn Abbas's view that this is the book God had told the Prophet He would send him.
[THALABI:v1p140/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · عطاء بن السائب | reports | Ata ibn al-Sa'ib says it is the book promised to the people on the covenant day.
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Taqwa derives from waqa, with initial waw changed to ta, as in taklan from waklan and takhma from wakhma.
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · بكر بن عبد الله | reports | Bakr ibn Abd Allah says a person is not pious until he guards against greed and anger.
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · عمر بن عبد العزيز | reports | Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz describes the muttaqi as someone mindful of what is forbidden, meaning within the sanctuary.
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · شهر بن حوشب | reports | Shahr ibn Hawshab says the pious person leaves what he cannot trust, wary of what may bring harm.
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r13] THALABI, d. 427 · النبي | reports | A report from the Prophet explains the name muttaqun by their leaving what is harmless lest they fall into what is harmful.
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r14] THALABI, d. 427 · سفيان الثوري والفضيل | reports | Sufyan al-Thawri and al-Fudayl define piety as loving for others what one loves for oneself.
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r15] THALABI, d. 427 · الجنيد بن محمد | prefers | Junayd ibn Muhammad goes further than Sufyan and al-Fudayl: the pious person loves for others more than he loves for himself; he illustrates this with al-Sari's concern that another receive most of the mercy for returning a greeting.
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله | reports | The Prophet says the comprehensive definition of taqwa is found in God's command to justice and excellence. | mentions 16:90
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas defines the God-fearing as those who avoid associating partners with God, major sins, and sexual indecencies.
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn Umar says piety means not seeing oneself as better than anyone else.
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says the God-fearing person considers everyone he sees better than himself.
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · كعب الأحبار | reports | Ka'b explains piety through Umar's image of carefully traversing a thorny path; Ibn al-Mu'tazz's poem extends it to avoiding both small and great sins.
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن المعتز | reports | Ibn al-Mu'tazz's poem says piety means leaving small and great sins, treading carefully over thorns, and not belittling small wrongs because mountains are made of pebbles.
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · عمر بن عبد العزيز | reports | Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz says piety is not merely daytime and nighttime worship; it is avoiding what God forbids and doing what He requires, with further provision being added goodness.
[THALABI:v1p142#2/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · طلق بن حبيب | reports | Taliq ibn Habib defines piety as acting in God's light while hoping for reward and leaving disobedience in God's light while fearing punishment.
[THALABI:v1p142/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Huda is a predicate, understood as huwa hudan, and the sentence ends at fihi; alternatively it is an accusative circumstantial, meaning the book guides the God-fearing and has no doubt in its guidance to them.
[THALABI:v1p142/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · أهل المعاني | reports | The specialists in meaning say the phrase is outwardly a negation but inwardly a prohibition: do not doubt the guidance and clarification by which a person is guided and sees clearly, like negations that prohibit during pilgrimage. | mentions 2:197
[THALABI:v1p143/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · محمد بن علي الترمذي | reports | Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi defines the pious person as one who has no adversary.
[THALABI:v1p143/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · الفضيل | reports | Al-Fudayl says a servant is pious when even his enemy feels as safe with him as his friend does.
[THALABI:v1p143/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · سهل | reports | Sahl defines the pious person as one who disowns his own power and strength.
[THALABI:v1p143/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · سهل | reports | Sahl also defines piety as not being found where God has forbidden and not being absent where He has commanded.
[THALABI:v1p143/r13] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Another definition is following the Prophet.
[THALABI:v1p143/r14] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Another account describes guarding the heart from heedlessness, the soul from desires, the throat from pleasures, and

[THALABI:v1p143/r15] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو القاسم الحكيم | reports | Abu al-Qasim al-Hakim defines piety as good character.
[THALABI:v1p143/r16] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | One view identifies three signs of piety: trusting well concerning what one has not attained, being content with what one has attained, and patiently accepting what has passed.
[THALABI:v1p143/r17] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Another definition is avoiding obedience to one's own desires.
[THALABI:v1p143/r18] THALABI, d. 427 · مالك | reports | Malik transmits that Medinan jurists wrote to Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr listing patience during affliction, acceptance of God's decree, gratitude for blessings, and submission to Quranic judgments as signs of the pious.
[THALABI:v1p143/r19] THALABI, d. 427 · ميمون بن مهران | reports | Maymun ibn Mihran says a person is not pious until he scrutinizes himself more strictly than a miserly partner or unjust ruler would.
[THALABI:v1p143/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · السري بن المفلس | reports | Al-Sari ibn al-Mufallis says the pious person is one who dislikes himself.
[THALABI:v1p143/r20] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو تراب | reports | Abu Turab lists five hurdles to piety: choosing austerity over ease, restraint over excess speech, humility over honor, exertion over comfort, and death over life.
[THALABI:v1p143/r21] THALABI, d. 427 · بعض الحكماء | reports | Some sages say a person reaches the summit of piety only if he would feel no shame were his inner thoughts displayed in the marketplace.
[THALABI:v1p143/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · الشبلي | reports | Al-Shibli defines piety as seeking what is less than God.
[THALABI:v1p143/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · جعفر الصادق | reports | Ja'far al-Sadiq cites Labid's verse, Every thing apart from God is false, as the Arabs' truest saying.
[THALABI:v1p143/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · الثوري | reports | Al-Thawri defines the pious person as one who avoids the world and its least share.
[THALABI:v1p143/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · محمد بن يوسف المقري | reports | Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Muqri defines piety as avoiding everything that distances one from God.
[THALABI:v1p143/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · القاسم بن القاسم | reports | Al-Qasim ibn al-Qasim defines piety as preserving the etiquette of the sacred law.
[THALABI:v1p143/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو زيد | reports | Abu Zayd defines piety as scrupulously avoiding all doubtful matters.
[THALABI:v1p143/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو زيد | reports | Abu Zayd also says the pious person speaks, is silent, and remembers only for God's sake.
[THALABI:v1p144/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | One definition of piety is to make one's inner self as beautiful for God as one's public self is for other people.
[THALABI:v1p144/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو الدرداء | reports | Abu al-Darda's poem contrasts human desire with God's will and says that piety is the best gain a person can acquire.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p67#2/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The Book guides people away from error.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p67#2/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الحسن البصري | reports | Hasan al-Basri defines the God-conscious as those who avoid God's prohibitions and fulfill His obligations.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p67#2/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas defines them as those who fear God's punishment and hope for His mercy.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p67#2/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | rejects | A third definition is those who avoid shirk and hypocrisy; al-Mawardi rejects it because such a person could still be sinful.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p67#2/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Although it guides everyone, the Qur'an is specially called guidance for the God-conscious because they believe and affirm its contents.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p67/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | One view identifies the Book as the Torah and Gospel, making the statement a report about the past.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p67/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الأصم | reports | Al-Asamm takes it as the Qur'an revealed before this passage in Mecca and Medina.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p67/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A third view means this Book; although dhalika normally indicates something absent, it can point to something present, as Khafaf ibn Nudba's verse shows.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p67/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | If the Book means Torah and Gospel, one view addresses the Prophet: the promised book mentioned there is what was sent to Muhammad.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p67/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | The other view addresses the Jews and Christians: the book promised to them is the one sent to Muhammad.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p67/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas explains rayb as doubt; a verse by Abd Allah ibn al-Zibara is cited as evidence.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p67/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A second lexical sense is accusation or suspicion, illustrated by Jamil's address to Buthayna.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p17/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · النبي | reports | The Prophet says he was given comprehensive expressions, so his speech was made concise.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p17/r10] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · أنشدوا | reports | Anonymous verses portray letters from beloveds as a cure for concealed pain and a source of joy, illustrating the friends’ comfort in their written message.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p17/r11] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Guidance means clarification, proof, light, and a clear path for those God protects from ignorance, enlightens with reason, and chooses for the realities of union.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p17/r12] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The Book heals God’s friends but blinds and afflicts His enemies.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p17/r13] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The Godfearing person does not rely on seeing his own piety and recognizes that salvation comes only through his Lord’s grace.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p17/r2] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · بعضهم | reports | An unnamed Sufi renders the opening letters as a compressed exchange between a lover and his master, ending in lam-alif.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p17/r3] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · قيل | reports | One explanation takes “that Book” to mean this very Book.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p17/r4] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · قيل | reports | Another explanation makes the phrase point to the discourse revealed earlier.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p17/r5] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · قيل | reports | Another view identifies the Book as the revelation God promised the Prophet on the Day of the Covenant.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p17/r6] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · قيل | reports | One view identifies the Book as the writing in which God promised mercy for Muhammad’s community; its certainty calls for trust in that promise.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p17/r7] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · قيل | reports | Another view reads the Book as God’s prior decree, fixed from eternity for those destined for felicity or misery.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p17/r8] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · قيل | reports | A further view says the certain divine decree is that God’s mercy preceded His wrath.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p17/r9] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · قيل | reports | The Book can signify faith, gnosis, love, and beneficence inscribed in the hearts of God’s friends; their absent beloved’s letters console and heal them.
[QUSHAYRI:v1p295/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The Qur’an benefits and guides the pious, and its warning is especially effective for them; fear here means knowledge, since the ignorant do not experience it. | mentions 2:2
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p10/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · من قال إنها أسماء للسور والقرآن | reports | On the same view, the letters may be a fronted predicate meaning the promised book is alif-lām-mīm.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p26#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو الهيثم | reports | Abu al-Haytham says ذا is the demonstrative for something present to speaker and listener, while adding kāf marks distance.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p26#2/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو الهيثم | reports | The added kāf is not an inflectional case ending; a following lām was added to avert the mistaken impression that kāf was genitive.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p26#2/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو الهيثم | reports | Abu al-Haytham says ذا is indeclinable in all cases because its demonstrative reference supplies a particle-like meaning; grammarians agree.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p26#2/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj explains the kasra on lām as resolving two adjacent sukūns; the Kufians do not discuss that kasra.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p26#2/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو الفتح الموصلي | reports | Abu al-Fath al-Mawsili treats lām as a permanently attached extra letter, adducing ذاك، أولئك، هناك and other forms whose shorter counterparts share their meanings.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p26#2/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو الفتح الموصلي | reports | The kāf in ذاك، ذلك، تلك، تانك، ذانك, and أولئك is an address particle, not a noun.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p26#2/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو الفتح الموصلي | reports | The dual retains its nūn before kāf; if kāf were a noun in iḍāfa, nūn would drop and kāf would be genitive.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p26#2/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Arabic also adds kāf as an address particle, as in النجاءك; commands do not take the commanded person's pronoun as an object.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p33/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari identifies the book as the revelation God had promised to send to Muhammad.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p33/r10] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | A further parse makes alif-lām-mīm one subject, ذلك another, الكتاب its predicate, and the whole clause predicate of the first.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p33/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · يمان بن رباب | reports | Yaman ibn Rabab says this is the book mentioned in the Torah and Gospel.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p33/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari links the demonstrative to God's prior promise to reveal weighty words, which the later revelation recalled to the Prophet. | mentions 73:5, 2:1
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p33/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p33/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس، والحسن، وقتادة، ومجاهد، والضحاك، ومقاتل | reports | Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil identify the book as the Qur'an.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p33/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Here al-kitāb denotes the written object, as in calling what is created al-khalq, rather than the act of creating or originating.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p33/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | prefers | He prefers the broad sense of the written revelation over naming it for prescribed obligations, since not all revelation imposes duties.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p33/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | If alif-lām-mīm connects to what follows, it can be the subject with ذلك its predicate and الكتاب an explanation.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p33/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | If alif-lām-mīm is separate, ذلك begins a clause whose predicate is هدى.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p36/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · جمهور أهل اللغة | reports | The majority of linguists distinguish rābanī, which indicates established suspicion, from arābanī, which raises suspicion without confirming it.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p36/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh says arāba means becoming a person of suspicion, like alāma meaning deserving blame; rābanī means making someone suspicious.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p36/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو زيد | reports | Abu Zayd distinguishes certainty of suspicion with rābanī from an unconfirmed suspicion with arābanī.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p36/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · قوم | reports | Some people treat rāba and arāba as synonymous, adducing a line by a Hudhali poet.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p36/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الأزهري | prefers | Al-Azhari sides with the expert distinction and Abu Zayd's account of rāba versus arāba.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p36/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh says لا governs its noun in the accusative without nunation, like إن, because it asserts negation as إن asserts affirmation.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p36/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh treats لا and its noun as one unit, a complete answer to a question about whether any person is present.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p39/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | La rajula gives a comprehensive class-wide negation, unlike hal rajul or la rajul, which only deny one and could allow two; lā rayba is comprehensive too.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p39/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh parses لا ريب as nominative in position as a subject, like خمسة عشر at sentence start; this permits a raised conjunction.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p39/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The poem لا أم لي إن كان ذاك ولا أب uses a raised conjunct by syntactic position; accusative conjunction instead follows the surface form.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p39/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | فِيهِ may be the predicate of لا ريب, or an adjective for ريب with an implied predicate such as واقع.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p39/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | If فيه is predicate it is nominative for two reasons; if adjectival, its case follows either the surface accusative or the syntactic nominative, as in poetic alternatives.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p39/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | If فيه is an adjective rather than a predicate, grammarians differ between following the surface accusative and the construction's syntactic nominative.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p39/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathir lengthens the pronoun hāʾ, adding a glide after it, including when the pronoun is nominative as in minhu and ʿanhu.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p39/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الباقون | reports | The other readers use only the short kasra or damma; the weak hāʾ is not counted as a barrier between adjacent quiescent sounds.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p53/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The form تقاك is analyzed as deriving from اتقاك by dropping its assimilated first consonant and then the connecting hamza; yattaqī similarly reflects a fuller form.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p53/r10] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari compares this omission to verses saying garments protect from heat and that not all People of the Book are alike, implying the unmentioned counterpart. | mentions 16:81, 3:113
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p53/r11] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو ذؤيب | reports | Abu Dhu'ayb's line leaves out the alternative 'or misguidance' after asking whether his beloved's pursuer is guided.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p53/r12] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Another verse calls the Qur'an guidance for all people; calling it guidance for the pious does not deny its guidance to others. | mentions 2:185
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p53/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الأزهري | reports | Al-Azhari derives اتقى from an original اوتقى, with wāw assimilating into tā; تقى means to meet something with something and thereby guard oneself.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p53/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · السكري | reports | Al-Sukkari calls the form taqā-yattaqī with open tā highly irregular, since comparable verbs do not drop their initial consonant.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p53/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الأزهري | reports | Al-Azhari says taqiya-yattaqī means to become pious.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p53/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أهل التفسير | reports | The exegetes identify the muttaqīn here as believers; the Qur'an guides those who avoided associating partners with God.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p53/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | A believer who still commits major sins remains among the muttaqīn here because he has faith in the Book and avoids shirk.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p53/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The Qur'an is guidance in itself for anyone who reflects, but is specifically called guidance for believers because they benefit from it while disbelievers do not.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p53/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The wording resembles the Prophet being called a warner to those who fear, though he warned both those who fear and those who do not. | mentions 79:45
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p53/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari understands the phrase as guidance for both the pious and disbelievers, with one party omitted though implied.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p55/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abu Ishaq parses هدى as an accusative circumstantial from الكتاب, with the demonstrative's meaning as its governor.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p55/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abu Ishaq also allows هدى to be an accusative circumstantial from the pronoun in فيه, governed by the meaning of ريب.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p55/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra calls the accusative qatʿ: الكتاب is the predicate of ذلك, and indefinite هدى is detached after a definite rather than explaining it.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p55/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra also permits detaching هدى from the pronoun in فيه, yielding 'no doubt in it, guiding.'
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p55/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abu Ishaq permits nominative هدى as a second predicate: the Book is both the promised Book and guidance, like something both sweet and sour.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p55/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Another nominative analysis supplies an omitted هو after the preceding statement: 'it is guidance.'
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p55/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | A pause after لا ريب treats that phrase as 'the Book is truly certain'; فيه هدى then begins a new clause.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v2p55/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The claim no doubt is objectively true even though false disputants doubt it; the cited poem likewise denies doubt in truth despite the liar's claims.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:1-2/r2] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | That book means this book, namely the Quran.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:1-2/r3] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | There is no doubt in it: it is true and right.

[DAMGHANI:v1p212/r8] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Rayb means doubt, as in “no doubt in it” and other verses denying doubt. | mentions 2:23, 3:25
[JISHUMI:v1p222/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · قيل | rejects | An unnamed view treats the initials as a secret whose intended meaning is unknowable; Jishumi rejects it because revelation aims to be understood and early scholars interpreted them, so it conflicts with their consensus.
[JISHUMI:v1p222/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Muttaqī derives from taqwā and protection; taqwā is a barrier between things, as when someone shields himself with armor, and the root wāw changes to tāʾ.
[JISHUMI:v1p222/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathir lengthens the pronoun ending in fīhi, ladayhi, ʿalayhi and similar forms; Ḥafṣ agrees in fīhi mahānan, while the others omit the yāʾ.
[JISHUMI:v1p222/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Arabic permits four forms here: with wāw, with yāʾ, or either short form; the underlying form is fīhū, and the faint hāʾ makes the sequence behave like yāʾ plus wāw, where wāw regularly turns to yāʾ, as in sayyid and mayyit.
[JISHUMI:v1p222/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | prefers | Jishumi prefers the common short reading because it is lighter without omitting a sound.

[JISHUMI:v1p222/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Hādhā points to what is near and dhāka to what is far; dhā is the noun, the lām is connective support, and the kāf marks address.
[JISHUMI:v1p222/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Kitāb derives from gathering, like a troop whose members assemble; literally it joins meaningful letters, and though a verbal noun it means the written thing, like ḥisāb or a dirham struck by the ruler.

[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#3/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | “That Book” means this Book, the Quran.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#3/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | An alternative supplies an omitted phrase: “this is that Book.”
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#3/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ says God had promised the Prophet in the Torah, Gospel, and through earlier prophets a Book that water could not erase and repeated recitation could not wear out; the Quran is that promised Book.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#3/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ explains “this” as indicating nearness and “that” as indicating distance.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#3/r5] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · ابن كيسان | reports | Ibn Kaysān takes “that Book” to mean the surahs preceding al-Baqara, which the polytheists had rejected and which contain no doubt.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#3/r6] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Kitāb is a verbal noun used to mean something written, as khalq can mean something created and ḍarb a thing struck by someone.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#3/r7] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The root sense of kitāb is joining and gathering; a troop is called a katība because its members gather, and a book joins letter to letter.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#4/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | There is no doubt that the Quran is from God and is the truth.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#4/r10] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | A hadith says that in intense battle the Companions sheltered behind the Messenger, illustrating taqwā as a protective barrier.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#4/r11] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · عمر بن الخطاب | reports | When ʿUmar asked Kaʿb about taqwā, Kaʿb compared it to carefully gathering oneself while crossing a thorny path.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#4/r12] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · شهر بن حوشب | reports | Shahr ibn Ḥawshab says the pious leave what is harmless for fear of what is harmful.

[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#4/r14] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | Another definition is following the Prophet; a hadith gathers the essence of taqwā in God's command to justice and excellence at 16:90. | mentions 16:90
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#4/r15] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn ʿUmar defines taqwā as not seeing oneself as better than anyone else.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#4/r16] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | The pious are singled out either to honor them or because they are the ones who benefit from guidance.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#4/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | An alternative reads the statement as a prohibition: “Do not doubt it,” like the prohibition in 2:197 against indecent conduct and disobedience. | mentions 2:197
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#4/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathir lengthens the pronominal hāʾ in connected recitation when preceded by a consonant and not followed by another consonant; after yāʾ he lengthens with kasra, otherwise with ḍamma, and Ḥafṣ agrees at 25:69. | mentions 25:69
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#4/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · أبو جعفر وابن كثير وحمزة والكسائي | reports | These readers assimilate ghunna before lām and rā; Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī add yāʾ, and Ḥamza adds wāw, while the others do not assimilate it.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p59#4/r5] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · أبو جعفر | reports | Abū Jaʿfar conceals nūn and tanwīn before khāʾ and ghayn.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p57/r17] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | A grammarian’s claim that only surā, bukā, and hudā are verbal nouns on the fuʿlā pattern is incorrect; Arabic also has liqā for meeting.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p58/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | In ittaqā, wāw changes to tāʾ and is then deleted after the hamzat al-waṣl, leaving taqā; this is a standard morphology topic.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p60#2/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The demonstrative ذلك is a remote demonstrative; the author sees no need to reinterpret it as “this,” as some do.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p61/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | The author chooses to parse ذلك الكتاب as a complete independent subject-and-predicate sentence, since Arabic allows it without ellipsis or dependence.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p61/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | His general method is to choose the most eloquent, least forced Arabic parsing rather than assign God’s speech every possibility accepted for poetry; alternatives are included for consideration.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p61/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قوم | reports | One parse supplies an omitted subject, “it is that Book,” with al-kitāb as adjective, apposition, or clarifying noun; another makes ذلك the subject and what follows its predicate.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p61/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قوم | reports | The clause lā rayba fīhi can stand independently or serve as the predicate of the demonstrative; al-kitāb can then be an adjective, apposition, clarifier, or further predicate.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p62/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | In the nominative reading, the form itself may suggest either comprehensive negation or denial of only one instance; context makes the intended meaning comprehensive.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p62/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Raising rīb could make it a subject with fīhi as predicate, or let lā work like laysa; the author considers the latter analysis weak because this use of lā is rare, so he calls the reading weak.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p62/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن أبي إسحاق | reports | Ibn Abī Isḥāq reads the hāʾ with ḍamma and links it with a wāw.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p62/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Fīhi might be the predicate of lā, a predicate with its noun under Sibawayh’s analysis, an adjective with an omitted predicate, or attached to rīb by an implied verb; the last makes lā’s noun extended and declinable.

[SAMIN-DURR:2:1-2#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The far demonstrative may honor the referent; other proposed reasons are its descent from heaven, its prior promise to the Prophet, or its decree in the Preserved Tablet. The author says the referent is mentally or physically present.

[SAMIN-DURR:2:1-2#8/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | A poetic counterexample attributed in the preceding segment to Alqama describes worldly wine as not causing headache or heaviness, but the author says it is no valid rebuttal because the poet's description carries no authority.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:1-2#8/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The best answer is that the Quran is not a proper object of doubt: fair-minded readers find decisive evidence, while negligent doubt is disregarded.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:1-2#8/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A second answer restricts the negation to believers: there is no doubt in the Quran for them.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:1-2#8/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A third answer takes the declarative statement as a prohibition meaning do not doubt the Quran.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:1-2#8/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Muttaqin derives from muttaqiyin; the first of two yāʾs is deleted under the weight of the kasra, then one of the adjacent sukūns is removed; the word is an iftiʿāl form from protection.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:1-2#8/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | In iftiʿāl, an initial wāw or yāʾ changes to tāʾ when followed by the infix tāʾ, as in ittaʿada and ittasara; analogous hamza changes are rare.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:1-2#8/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Iftiʿāl has twelve uses, including adoption, causation, reflexive action, selection, snatching, passive counterparts, reciprocal or intensive equivalents, equivalence to a simple verb, and replacing an unattested simple form.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:1-2#8/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Wiqaya means intense protection and caution against harm, illustrated by a horse that protects its hoof; another view says its original sense is little speech.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:1-2#8/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The saying al-muttaqi muljam presents the God-fearing person as restrained; the cited poetry illustrates shielding or covering oneself with the hand.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:1-2#9/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A second poem uses ittaqat in the sense of shielding oneself behind joined hands and forearm.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p162#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | holds | Ibn Abbas and the named early authorities understand dhālika here as ‘this’; Ibn Kathir endorses them and says Arabic uses these two demonstratives interchangeably.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p162#2/r10] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | prefers | Ibn Kathir prefers pausing after ‘no doubt in it’; then ‘guidance’ directly describes the Qur’an, which is more emphatic than saying guidance is in it. | mentions 32:1, 32:2
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p162#2/r11] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | From the perspective of Arabic grammar, huda may be nominative as an adjective or accusative as a circumstantial expression.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p162#2/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Al-rayb means doubt; Ibn Kathir cites al-Suddi, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Masud, many others, and says Ibn Abi Hatim knows no disagreement.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p164/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Taqwa is guarding oneself against what one dislikes; its root comes from wiqaya, protection.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p164/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Al-Nabigha and another poet use forms of the root for shielding oneself, illustrating taqwa as protection.

[BURHAN:v1p100/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | Opening letters can be counted as verses because they stand independently and fit rhyme, or excluded because their lengths vary and they syntactically attach to what follows.

[BURHAN:v1p348/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | prefers | Following the Prophetic practice of stopping at verse endings is preferable even when syntax continues; al-Akhfash likewise recommended a stop after هدى للمتقين because it ends a verse.
[BURHAN:v1p50/r9] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | Grammarians differ: some parse فيه هدى as an independent subject and predicate; others make فيه the predicate of لا and هدى a circumstantial accusative meaning هاديا.

[BURHAN:v3p154/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | An adjective can stand without its noun only when it uniquely identifies that noun and the context is focused on the adjective; Sibawayh and Aristotle state the first condition.
[BURHAN:v3p154/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | In praise or blame, context can focus on the adjective alone, allowing omission of the described noun; guidance for the pious means guidance for the pious people.

[BIQAI-FULL:v1p31#s002/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The transition from al-Fatiha's plea for the straight path to al-Baqara identifies that guidance with this Book, then describes the guided and rejected groups to teach the path to follow and the path to avoid.

[DURR-FULL:v1p59/r6] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masʿūd glosses Alif-Lām-Mīm as a letter of God's name, al-kitāb as the Quran, and lā rayba as no doubt.
[DURR-FULL:v1p59/r7] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, with ʿIkrima transmitting the same gloss, explains dhālika al-kitāb as this book.

[YKHULI-TAJDID:c1/f39] YKHULI-TAJDID · أمين الخولي | holds | For al-Khuli, renewal answers changing life and needs, extends the vitality of texts, and realizes the adaptive purpose of ijtihād without requiring changes to Islamic creed.

[YKHULI-TAJDID:c1/f45] YKHULI-TAJDID · أمين الخولي | holds | Because the six-day creation of each species and divine rest appear only in Genesis, al-Khuli calls the alleged conflict between Islam and evolution a fabrication of intrusive Israelite traditions.
[YKHULI-TAJDID:c1/f46] YKHULI-TAJDID · أمين الخولي | holds | Al-Khuli links religious renewal with linguistic renewal: language expresses collective existence, religion gives it direction, grammar's old foundations rest on jurisprudence, and rhetoric studies the Qur'an's exemplary speech.
